The post The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.

Actual Article Body:
A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

At some point in the past three decades, a beer can printed with a Spanish-language ad for a 1990s World Cup washed up on Patroklos, a small islet in the Saronic Gulf about 65 nautical miles (75 miles) from Athens. No swimmer left it there. Like most of what collects on Greece’s harder-to-reach shores, it rode in on the currents, and it stayed until a crew working on a Greek coastline cleanup picked it up, sorted it, and wrote it down. That last step, the writing down, is what makes this project more interesting than a beach sweep. Every bottle, net, and wrapper the crew logs becomes a clue about where the Mediterranean’s waste starts its trip.

Greece has the longest coastline of any Mediterranean country, and much of it has no road leading to it. Since July 2019, the Typhoon Project has reached those stretches by water, using a 72-meter (236-foot) ship as its base. Each day, a crew of 20 heads ashore in five inflatable boats and gathers, sorts, and records between 500 and 1,000 kilograms (roughly 1,100 to 2,200 pounds) of waste, which then goes to the appropriate facilities for recycling.

The project belongs to the Public Benefit Foundation Athanassios C. Laskaridis, a Greek foundation whose work centers on protecting the environment and the sea in particular. By February 2023, the crew had completed its first full circuit of the islands and most of the mainland coast.

Across more than 10,000 cleanup operations, the Typhoon has removed 1,140 tonnes (about 1,257 US tons) of trash. Peggy Xirotagarou, the foundation’s executive director, has learned that the number means more to people as an image than as a weight. “To help people picture it in their minds, we are talking about 22 Olympic-size swimming pools or around 1160 large containers,” she said.

The cleanup is half the job. The other half happens after the bags are on board, when the crew records what was found, item by item and beach by beach. Thanasis Besios, who manages the Typhoon Project, considers that record as valuable as the cleared sand. “One part of the project is collecting the waste, but the second is collecting the data. We carry out detailed recording of all the waste. We know exactly what quantity there is, how many kilos, how many items from each beach. At the moment we have the largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean, and we are developing it every day,” he told Euronews.
